title: The reformations, looking back
tomorrow: why does Hebrews call a crowd of runners a cloud?

cards: A group chat in the middle of a fight shows fast who's on which side. Now an older argument. A scholar named William Tyndale is arguing with a learned man about who should be allowed to read the Bible.

The story goes that Tyndale ends it with a promise: one day a boy driving a plow will know more scripture than you do. Then he leaves the country to keep it, putting the New Testament into English, in hiding.
And the people who don't want it in English are looking for him.

teach.b: They found him. Tyndale was put to death, and his English kept being read. That's the reformations, plural, because there was more than one, and every one had a cost.

teach.h: THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY FAITH.
teach.b: Martin Luther, a monk and teacher in Germany, read Paul's letter to the Romans and found a line that turned him around: “The just shall live by faith.”
He spoke out against what he saw as abuses in the church, and Protestant churches grew from that break.
Menno Simons, a priest in the Netherlands, joined the Anabaptists, who baptized believing adults and would not take up the sword.
And inside the Catholic Church, Teresa of Avila was reforming too, founding poorer, simpler convents given to prayer.
Looking back honestly, it was also a time of wounds. Christians on more than one side were imprisoned and killed by other Christians, and the family of churches split in ways that still ache.
Churches still tell the story differently.

Some keep a phrase about themselves: reformed and reforming, never finished being made new. And some churches now pray together, across those old lines, for what Paul asked: “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

how: Some Protestant churches mark a Reformation Sunday each fall, and some congregations from different churches pray together for Christian unity in a week set aside for it each January.

games.q: two friends from different churches start arguing about who got the Reformation right. what does 'reformed and reforming' suggest?
o: pick the winner and settle it for good.
every church is still being made new; hear what the other side keeps.
never bring it up again; history only divides.
games.why: the phrase says no church is finished. Paul asks for the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, not a winner.

practice: Count on your fingers three people whose church or way is different from yours: a neighbor, a classmate, a relative. For each finger, name one good thing they bring that your own side might miss.
If you pray, end with a psalm's line: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.

wordCard.voice: The reformations. Luther, Teresa, Tyndale and Menno: more than one reform, real wounds, and churches still being made new.

orig.note: Latin: always being reformed. a phrase some Reformed churches use of themselves.
